billow

BIL-oh · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To billow is to rise, swell, or roll outward in large waves or masses, especially of smoke, cloth, or water.

Storm clouds billowed on the horizon, their dark shapes swelling higher by the minute as the wind picked up.

Worked Example

The curtains billowed inward every time someone opened the front door, catching the draft like a sail.

Billow describes something swelling or rolling outward in large waves, often because of wind or rising heat -- here, the curtains filled with air and puffed outward.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

surge: To surge is to move forward or upward in one powerful, sweeping push -- a crowd surges toward the stage, a wave surges up the shore. To billow is gentler and rounder: fabric or smoke swells outward in soft, wave-like masses instead of driving ahead with force.

swell: To swell is simply to grow larger or puff outward, and almost anything can swell -- an ankle, a river, bread dough. To billow is a particular way of swelling: loose, soft material like smoke, sails, or curtains filling and rolling outward in waves.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deflate: to collapse or lose its swollen shape

subside: to sink back down or become calmer

Where it sits · how big and forceful the movement is — flutter → billow → churn

flutter vs. billow: To flutter is to move with small, light flapping motions, a much gentler image than fully billowing outward.

churn vs. billow: To churn is to billow and roil with violent, turbulent motion, an even more intense and chaotic image than simply billowing.

Build the Word

The pieces

whole word (no productive root) — billow

whole word (no productive root) — billow: traced to Old Norse bylgja, meaning 'a wave' -- it entered English mostly unchanged and never grew a family of related English words (Old Norse bylgja)

Put it together

Put it together: Billow comes from Old Norse bylgja, simply meaning 'a wave.' Unlike many of this unit's words, it didn't grow a family of related English words built on the same root -- it's essentially the same word English borrowed centuries ago, still describing something swelling and rolling like a wave.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Billow came from Old Norse bylgja, 'a wave,' and has stayed a loner ever since: English never built other words on its root. Its meaning barely moved either -- what billows today still swells and rolls the way the Norse wave did.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Billow is almost always used for things that move in large, soft, wave-like swells -- smoke, sails, clouds, fabric -- rather than for solid objects; you wouldn't say a rock billowed.
